title: Genesis 9. The Cup Sealed.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 9. The Cup Sealed.
God blesses Noah and his sons.
The same words: Be fruitful.
Multiply.
Fill the earth.
What God spoke in chapter one, He speaks again,
now to a world that has been drowned and has dried.
The blessing has survived the flood.
But something has changed.
The fear of man will now be on every animal.
The dread of man, on every beast, every bird, every fish.
They are delivered into man's hand.
In chapter one,
man was given dominion over creatures who had no reason to fear him.
Now they do.
The Cup that held harmony has been refilled with a fracture.
Man rules, but the creatures he rules are afraid of him.
Every moving thing that lives shall be food for you.
As I gave you the green herb, I give you everything.
The boundary that was set in chapter one,
when God gave every green plant for food to man and beast alike,
is now widened.
Man may eat flesh.
But the blood, the life, belongs to God.
You shall not eat flesh with its life, that is, its blood.
The Cup that was poured out in the flood now carries a restriction.
Life is not man's to consume.
Blood is not food.
It is the carrier of life, and life is God's.
The flood has not made life cheap.
It has made it sacred.
The first dietary law in Scripture is not about cleanliness.
It is about custody.
Life belongs to God.
And I will require a reckoning.
At the hand of every animal.
At the hand of man.
At the hand of every man's brother.
Whoever sheds man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed,
for God made man in His own image.
The image given in chapter one is reaffirmed after the flood.
But now the image carries a consequence.
The blood that cried from the ground in chapter four, Abel's blood,
crying to God, is now answered with a law:
blood will be required.
The violence that filled the earth before the flood is now met with a boundary.
If man sheds blood, his blood will be shed.
The Cup that was emptied by violence is now guarded by law.
Then God speaks the covenant.
Behold, I establish My covenant with you and your offspring after you.
With every living creature that is with you, the birds, the livestock,
every animal.
Never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of the flood.
Never again shall there be a flood to destroy the earth.
The covenant spoken inside judgment in chapter six is now sealed.
The Cup of judgment is closed with a word.
And the word carries a sign.
I set My bow in the cloud.
The bow appears in the cloud.
The Hebrew word can name a bow used as a weapon,
which allows the image of a weapon set aside,
but Genesis itself calls the bow the sign of covenant.
God says He will look at it and remember the everlasting covenant.
The Cup now holds restraint:
the waters will not again become a flood to destroy all flesh.
The Cup is sealed.
Then the scene turns.
Noah begins to be a man of the soil.
He plants a vineyard.
He drinks the wine.
He is drunk.
He lies uncovered in his tent.
The Cup, which has been creation, fall, blood, flood, ark, covenant, rainbow,
now becomes wine for the first time in Scripture.
And the first use of wine is excess.
The righteous man, the one who walked with God,
the one who found grace, lies exposed.
The vessel that survived the flood cracks in a tent with a cup in his hand.
The same pattern as Eden, abundance given, boundary set, boundary crossed.
But the boundary this time was not commanded.
Noah was not told: do not drink.
He simply drank too much.
Ham, the father of Canaan, sees his father's nakedness.
He does not cover him.
He tells his two brothers outside.
The transparency of chapter two, naked and not ashamed,
has been gone since chapter three.
What returns here is not Eden's transparency.
It is exposure without dignity.
The father who was covered by God's skins in chapter three is now uncovered by his own son's gaze.
And the son does what the serpent did in chapter three:
he takes what he has seen and makes it known.
He does not protect.
He exposes.
Shem and Japheth take a garment.
They lay it on their shoulders.
They walk backward.
They cover their father's nakedness.
Their faces are turned away.
They do not see it.
The covering.
The same movement as chapter three, nakedness exposed, shame entering through seeing,
covered by others who will not look.
God covered Adam and Eve with skins that cost an animal's life.
Shem and Japheth cover their father with a garment that costs their own dignity,
walking backward, refusing to see, preserving what their brother exposed.
Noah wakes.
He knows what his youngest son has done to him.
He curses Canaan, Ham's son.
Not Ham himself.
Canaan.
The curse falls on the next generation.
The Cup passes down again, carrying both the covenant and the fracture,
the rainbow and the curse, the blessing and the servitude.
What Noah speaks over his sons will shape the nations that come from them.
Blessed be the Lord, the God of Shem.
Let Canaan be his servant.
May God enlarge Japheth.
Let him dwell in the tents of Shem.
Let Canaan be his servant.
Shem is blessed.
Japheth is enlarged.
Canaan is cursed.
From three sons, the whole earth is populated,
and the whole earth carries what was spoken in this tent.
The covenant that God sealed with a bow in the sky is answered by a man lying drunk in a tent,
a son who exposed what he saw,
two sons who covered what they refused to see,
and a curse that will follow a grandson into the land that will later be called Canaan.
Noah lives three hundred and fifty years after the flood.
All his days are nine hundred and fifty years.
And he died.
The drumbeat from chapter five, the one that broke for Enoch,
that held through Methuselah and Lamech,
sounds for the last time on the man who carried the Cup through the flood.
The man who found grace.
The man who walked with God.
The man who built an altar.
The man who planted a vineyard.
The man who lay uncovered.
Nine hundred and fifty years.
And he died.
The Cup that was sealed with a rainbow passes into the hands of three sons,
one blessed, one cursed, one enlarged.
What they will do with it has not yet been seen.
